messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Model
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Marguerite Calloway is a sixty-six-year-old widowed woman who has worked as a professional model for most of her adult life, a career that has taken her from regional catalogue shoots in her thirties to, more recently, editorial work for brands targeting older consumers. She presents for an initial psychological evaluation approximately fourteen months after an incident in which she accidentally struck a pedestrian with her vehicle, causing the woman serious and lasting physical injury. Marguerite's PCL-5 score of 41 places her within the clinical range for PTSD, and the picture that emerges across intake and early sessions is one of a woman who has not had a single uncomplicated day since the afternoon the accident occurred.

It happened on a Tuesday in late autumn, just after dusk. Marguerite had been leaving a studio fitting on the outskirts of the city, running slightly behind, distracted by a phone call she had just ended. The light was poor and the pedestrian — a middle-aged woman — had stepped from between two parked delivery vans into the road. The impact was immediate and the sound, Marguerite has said more than once, was something she cannot locate language for. She stayed at the scene. She called for help. She held the woman's hand until the ambulance arrived. The woman survived but sustained a fractured pelvis and spinal damage that required months of rehabilitation and left her with a permanent limp.

In the weeks that followed, Marguerite found herself returning obsessively to a single question: why had she not slowed down sooner? She had been on a familiar stretch of road. She had driven it dozens of times. What frightened her most was not the memory of the impact itself but the conviction, which had settled into her like something calcified, that another person — a more careful person, a more attentive person — would never have been in that situation at all. She had come to believe that the accident revealed something essential and damning about her character, a conclusion she held with a certainty that no reassurance from friends or her attorney had been able to touch. She felt permanently humiliated, not only by the public nature of the incident — there had been a brief local news item — but by what she understood it to say about who she was. She was certain she would never forgive herself for not having done more in those seconds before impact, even as she acknowledged, in a quieter part of herself, that there had been almost no time at all.

Her body has remained in a state of readiness that exhausts her. She cannot sit still through a meal or a television programme. Her muscles carry a tension she notices most acutely in her shoulders and jaw, and she has described lying in bed at night feeling as though her body is braced for something that has not yet arrived. Concentration has become unreliable in ways that have begun to affect her professionally. During shoots — which she has continued, in part because work has always been a source of structure — she loses the thread of a director's instruction mid-sentence, has to ask for things to be repeated, and has noticed the barely concealed impatience of colleagues who knew her previously as composed and precise. Last spring, a booking she had held for several months was quietly reassigned to another model. No formal explanation was given, but Marguerite understood. She has said nothing about this to anyone.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her daughter, who visited in the autumn and told her, plainly and with evident worry, that she seemed like a different person. Marguerite did not disagree. She made the referral call the following week, though she spent several days beforehand rehearsing reasons not to. She arrives at sessions composed in the way of someone who has long been accustomed to being looked at, but beneath that composure she is carrying a grief she has not yet named — for the woman she injured, yes, but also for the version of herself she has not been able to find her way back to. What she hopes for, she has said, is to stop feeling like someone who is waiting to be punished. What she fears is that she deserves to wait.
